questions.q: What is the key limitation of Discretionary Access Control (DAC) that Mandatory Access Control (MAC) is designed to address?
options: DAC cannot be configured with chmod or chown
DAC is only available on Windows, not Linux
DAC and MAC are actually the same mechanism with different names
DAC access is controlled at the resource owner's discretion, and root bypasses DAC checks entirely
questions.explain: Under DAC, a process inherits whatever permissions its owning user has, and root isn't subject to DAC checks at all. MAC adds a system-wide policy layer that applies even to root.

questions.q: What does SELinux actually check when deciding whether to allow an action?
options: Only the file's standard owner/group/other permission bits
Whether the requesting user is in the sudoers file
The file's path and nothing else
The security context (user:role:type:level) attached to the process and the file, per policy rules on the type
questions.explain: SELinux labels both processes and files with a security context, and policy defines which process types may access which file types — independent of DAC permissions.

questions.q: What are SELinux's three modes, and what does each one do?
options: SELinux only has one mode: enforcing
Enforcing, permissive, and auditing — all three block violations but log differently
Enforcing (blocks and logs violations), permissive (logs only), and disabled (off entirely)
Enabled, confined, and unconfined, with no logging in any mode
questions.explain: getenforce/sestatus show the current mode; setenforce switches between enforcing and permissive at runtime, while /etc/selinux/config sets it permanently.

questions.q: How does an AppArmor profile differ from SELinux's approach to confining a program?
options: AppArmor profiles are path-based, naming a binary and listing files it may access by path, rather than using security-context labels
AppArmor only works on RHEL and CentOS
AppArmor profiles apply only to files, never to processes
AppArmor and SELinux both use identical security-context labeling
questions.explain: AppArmor, the default on Ubuntu/Debian/SUSE, confines a program with a plain-text profile in /etc/apparmor.d/ named after its path, rather than labeling files with security contexts.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, why can't a web shell running as the apache user read /etc/shadow on a RHEL server with SELinux enforcing?
options: /etc/shadow is deleted automatically whenever SELinux is enabled
The apache user's DAC permissions already prevent reading /etc/shadow, so SELinux isn't involved
Web shells cannot execute any commands on SELinux systems
SELinux policy never grants the httpd_t process type permission to access files labeled outside its allowed types, regardless of DAC permissions
questions.explain: SELinux confines the httpd_t type to a narrow set of allowed file types. Even though the compromised process runs as apache, MAC policy blocks the read independent of ownership-based DAC checks.
